To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
clinical examination and breast ultrasound are good at predicting residual disease, but not complete response.

clinical breast examination, digital mammogram, and breast ultrasound are not accurate in predicting pathologic complete response after neoadjuvancy therapy in patients with operable breast cancer, and that MRI has a higher accuracy and PPV than the other modalities, but its NPV remains poor.
clinical examination and imaging are good at predicting disease, but are unable to accurately predict complete response.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the accuracy, positive and negative predictive values of breast imaging modalities in the determination of pathologic complete response after neoadjuvants therapy in patients with locally invasive breast cancer.
the evaluation of breast cancer in the preoperative phase, with the aim of predicting the final histological result of surgical intervention.
the development of an efficient, accurate, and reliable method for predicting the pathologic response to neoadjuvant treatment of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all modalities, when used alone, are poor predictors of complete pathologic response in breast cancer.
none of the modalities evaluated is sufficiently sensitive and specific to be used as a stand-alone tool for the assessment of pathologic complete response.
none of the available tests are accurate enough to be used to guide treatment decisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MRI is the most sensitive test for detecting residual disease, but it is not sufficiently accurate for use in determining pathologic response.
MRI is the most accurate method to detect residual disease after neoadjuvants therapy, but it is unable to predict pathologic complete response.
the best test for determining residual disease is a combination of MRI and breast ultrasound.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NPV of all tests is low, and this should be considered when counseling patients about neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
the accuracy of breast imaging is compromised in younger patients.
the PPV and NPV of each imaging modality was compromised in patients younger than 40 years.
